results.title: Building a Robust Annotation Strategy for High-Quality ML Training Data | by Grace L | Medium
results.content: # Building a Robust Annotation Strategy for High-Quality ML Training Data. Annotation forms the foundation of supervised learning systems, and well-structured, consistent labeling is crucial for building reliable models. * **Annotation Guidelines**: Develop detailed instructions with clear definitions, labeled visual examples (correct and incorrect cases), edge case handling rules, and technical specifications (e.g., minimum bounding box size for images). * **Cross-Annotation Consistency**: Review visually or semantically similar inputs across batches to ensure annotators are applying labels uniformly. Have annotators label the data, then run automated comparisons with the ground truth and provide feedback. * **Active Learning Integration**: Use model uncertainty to prioritize which data should be labeled or reviewed next. After annotation, ensure your data is ML-ready:. If you’re building out a data operations pipeline or supporting ML teams with annotation workflows, feel free to adapt or remix this framework. *This article was originally published on* *IzzyBreezyLife: Building a Robust Annotation Strategy for High-Quality ML Training Data**.*.

results.content: cross lingual information retrieval Cross-Lingual Information Retrieval with Explicit Semantic Analysis Published: 2025-06-05T00:05:30.364Z Cross-language information retrieval (CLIR) has emerged as a pivotal technology for accessing information across language barriers, transforming the way we interact with multilingual content. Through an examination of Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA), Explicit Semantic Analysis (ESA), and advanced frameworks like HIKE that integrate multilingual Knowledge Graphs, we uncover the technical foundations and practical applications of modern cross-language retrieval systems. Introduction to Cross-Lingual Information Retrieval Cross-Lingual Information Retrieval (CLIR) represents a crucial advancement in multilingual information retrieval systems, enabling users to retrieve information across language barriers (Demner-Fushman et al. Traditional information retrieval systems are language-specific, either limited to finding documents in the query language or employing machine translation systems that lack effectiveness across languages (What is CLIR? These graphs enable explicit semantic analysis by linking queries to aligned entities in target languages, while mechanisms like Hierarchical Knowledge Enhancement (HIKE) combine information from multiple languages to improve query-document matching (HIKE [3]). Latent Semantic Analysis for Cross-Lingual Retrieval The Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) approach, while requiring parallel texts across languages to construct a multi-dimensional matrix, has proven effective for cross-lingual information retrieval by computing latent concepts from data (Demner-Fushman et al. The ESA framework extends traditional Latent Semantic Indexing by mapping both queries and documents into high-dimensional vector spaces, where each dimension corresponds to a Wikipedia article in multiple languages (Egoz et al. Experiments on the CLEF 2008 Ad-Hoc retrieval dataset showed consistent performance improvements when restricting Wikipedia article selection to those with cross-language links, suggesting that these links carry particularly relevant semantic information (Egoz et al. These systems typically employ one of two strategies: translating queries or documents into a common language or embedding both into a shared semantic space (How does cross-lingual IR work? By treating Wikipedia articles as dimensional bases, these systems can capture complex relationships between terms across languages (Cross-lingual Information Retrieval with Explicit Semantic Analysis [1]). ### Hierarchical Information Fusion The HIKE model employs a sophisticated hierarchical fusion approach that combines information from three distinct levels: knowledge, language, and query-document pairs (Figure 2).

results.content: Our goal is to define a cheap and replicable data collection methodology that minimizes the manual work done by expert annotators, without resorting to preprocessing tools or already annotated monolingual datasets. In line with recent works emphasizing the need of large-scale annotation efforts for textual entailment, our work aims to: i) tackle the scarcity of data available to train and evaluate systems, and ii) promote the recourse to crowdsourcing as an effective way to reduce the costs of data collection without sacrificing quality. We show that a complex data creation task, for which even experts usually feature low agreement scores, can be effectively decomposed into simple subtasks assigned to non-expert annotators. The resulting dataset, obtained from a pipeline of different jobs routed to Amazon Mechanical Turk, contains more than 1,600 aligned pairs for each combination of texts-hypotheses in English, Italian and German. plex task (i.e. creating and annotating entailment. entailment-annotated pairs) at a monolingual level. the entailment annotations of ENG/ENG1 pairs can. the pair was annotated as unidirectional entailment. Crowdsourcing can allow inexpensive and rapid data collection for various Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks [11], [12], [13], including human evaluations of NLP systems [14], [15], [16], [17], [18]. We study how Edit-MT fares with this new problem on two publicly available datasets: first on the SemEval 2012&3 Task 8: Cross-lingual Textual Entailment (CLTE, Negri et al., 2011Negri et al., , 2012Negri et al., , 2013, 14 then with the OpenSubtitles corpus (Lison and Tiedemann, 2016). The analysis of the results is performed by comparing the acquired data with the recognizing textual entailment (RTE) challenge dataset. As a result, an accurate and reliable corpus of 426 English/Spanish entailment pairs has been produced in a more cost-effective way com-pared to other methods for the acquisition of translations based on crowdsourcing. This paper presents the Third PASCAL Recognising Textual Entailment Challenge (RTE-3), providing an overview of the dataset creating methodology and the submitted systems. We use insights from successful RTE systems to propose a model for identifying and annotating textual inference phenomena in textual entailment examples, and we present the results of a pilot annotation study that show this model is feasible and the results immediately useful.
